I know the term "Game Design" gets thrown around a lot, like it's just a term for "idea man " or "someone that works on games", but I've always been fascinated by actual game design. What motivates players to do things, what makes something "fun" instead of just a goal... stuff like that.

I just turned 27, and I feel like the window for pursuing an actual career in the Gaming industry is going to wind up passing me by. As someone with little experience and zero formal training, or even a degree, I'm already "behind the curve". I suppose I'm wondering, has the time to pursue my "dream job" already passed me by? Or if not... How would you even approach it?

I've been tooling around with the Unreal 4 Engine off-and-on for the past few months, but my PC seems pretty well fubar (a local PC repair shop is checking it out now, but I'm not overly optimistic; I think there's something wrong with the motherboard, and I don't have the money to replace it), so I don't really know what my next move should be.

Try to pursue a degree, or even a certificate in "Game Design"? Or just continue familiarizing myself with UE4, and focus on making something you can actually play, even if it winds up being kind of shit as an actual game? (I can draw rough concept sketches, but I've never had a knack for making pleasant-looking art).

Also, hey; it's my first post on voat!
Any advice for someone interested in pursuing an actual career in game development, specifically Game Design?

It seems like there are a lot of tools and tutorials out there and available for free. If it was me, I'd start formulating specific ideas and then look into how to execute them. A degree might be good if you're looking to work on other peoples games. But it seems possible, especially if you have a solid idea, to do it yourself and reap all of the rewards (maybe even 2.5 B from Microsoft).

Let me tell you what I did: I met a bunch of people and tried to make something awesome. Here we are, about a year later, and FINALLY, about a month ago, it went from "wow this is much shittier than we could have ever imagined" to "holy shit, this game is my own idea AND I WANT TO PLAY IT".

I'm the Game Director for a small indie studio. My advice is if you're going to do it, expect to dedicate half a decade to it, work your own ass off, and find a group of people that believes in your idea. You'll go far.

If you mean the standard corporate game industry, yeah, your time is almost up. I'm just kidding, but the main thing they look for is Computer Science experience, whether from a degree or from the industry, and it's hard to get in that way.

Doing stuff yourself allows you to build whatever portfolio you want to make.

That's the repetitive advice on this page that I hope OP takes to heart. Just start doing stuff. Finding people has an element of luck too, and I say screw that. Don't wait for anybody to kiss your butt. Just start working that butt off instead. Having a "good game idea" is a totally different thing when it's mentioned by somebody who has actually made games.

These days, when indie studios start to break through, they seem to start trying shady crap to keep the ride going. Hiring people to shill up competitors' reviews or stink up their forums. I think character will go a long way for indie developers in years to come because we're almost at that critical point where practically everybody has seen the shady side of this stuff and gets sick of it.

Get a business degree, preferably master's. Learn everything you can about every aspect of development because you'll be coordinating it all. Practice every aspect of development so you're not that boss who doesn't know jack. Keep playing games in the meantime to keep up with the market without relying on the opinions of others. Finally, come up with a metric shit ton of cash despite now being in debt.

Or just start making games, get a little lucky, and then be a dick to make your own luck. Or just start making games, get a lot lucky, and have the luxury of being allowed to be nice. Or start making assets and selling them to other developers.

"Game Design" is not a field. It's what people say when they "want to make games" but they don't want to do any work. Everybody has an idea for a video game that they think is brilliant. That means less than nothing. Less than. As in, there are people who just might pay you to not talk about it if they were trapped in a stuck elevator with you.

Sorry if I'm raining on your parade. If you want to do something great for the game industry, focus on one component of the standard game engine -- one out of the potentially hundreds of subsystems -- and work at improving that one thing until you have something worthwhile. This will not be a play time task. I'm not saying that you should do the equivalent of fingerpaint in Blender for a few years or make a thousand variations of a Tetris clone or something. I mean, find the most boring, technical, math heavy part of game engines that hasn't changed in too long and advance that one thing. See ya in ten years.

But, yeah, nobody will pay you to sit around and think up awesome game ideas. Wishing for that is like wishing to be discovered and whisked off to Hollywood to be made a millionaire just for being you on camera. It's not going to happen. The sooner you forget it, the better off you are.

At this point, pursuing a game design degree is basically like throwing tens of thousands of dollars out in order to network. If you're good at self-teaching, I'd suggest just learning how to make games yourself. A better PC will be a much better use of your money, since one is virtually required if you plan on going for a degree as is.

You're already taking a step in the right direction by familiarizing yourself with UE4. So long as you can create playable titles, that should be enough to start building a portfolio with. If you can find an artist, great. But if you can't, just use placeholder models. So long as the mechanics and coding is there, such pieces should be just fine.

Unfortunately, you are quite a bit behind the curve. But it's certainly not too late to catch up. Keep learning UE4. Look at other engines/programs as well if you have the time. Start reading up on game design philosophy. Don't try to mimic it completely, but at least keep in it mind. Talk to people. Learn what they like in video games, what makes them tick. You may get some ideas that you may have never come up with alone.

I can answer any further questions if you'd like.

I'm where you are + a year or two.

I'm in my 30's and prior to January 2014 I knew zero code or how to make a game (with the exception of doing some level design for Wheel of Time and UT99 back in the 90s. Which was CAD and without code. User maps, not official or anything.)

So in January I decided to take up coding. I did the Python course at www.codeacademy.com which was insanely easy and that got me started. Then I got into Unity. Unity is less code heavy than Unreal AFAIK. Its scripting is done in C# or Javascript which is pretty simple (You can also do Javascript at codeacademy).

The trick to getting into game design is to just start making games. Don't try to make a huge idea, make a ton of small ideas. Your first game will be garbage, your first 10 games might be garbage, but you will get better and you'll have these old concepts to pull from. I'm bad right now about just making "Proof of Concept" games. Stuff that isn't even a full level. I'll spend a week or two creating a super basic design to try out an idea, once the idea works and its ready for Art and Sound and stuff, I move on.

My weakness is I'm not artistic at all. I can do basic photoshop and a little more than basic Blender modeling, but most everything looks like Potato. The scripting is easy to pick up (in Unity anyways) but can be a challenge to get perfect.

If you ever want to try working in Unity5 let me know. I've been dying to find some people to work with, particularly more art-centric people.
